title: Gateway capacity and admission control
description: The v2 view: what the gateway decides, and the two engine signals that predict when those decisions start hurting. Deliberately separate from the vLLM engine dashboard - this one only shows facts the engine cannot know, because they happen before a request reaches it.

panels.title: Client-observed TTFT (includes queue wait)
panels.description: The number a user actually feels. It includes time spent queued in the gateway, which vLLM's own TTFT histogram cannot see. The 1.5s threshold line is the stated SLO — and note it is defined for chat-length prompts of roughly 500 tokens; a workload of very long prompts breaches it legitimately.

panels.title: Admitted vs shed (requests/s)
panels.description: The graph that proves degradation is bounded. As offered load rises past capacity, admitted flattens and shed absorbs the excess — instead of both being accepted and everyone waiting. A non-zero shed rate under burst is correct behaviour, not an incident.

panels.title: In-flight vs queue depth vs limit
panels.description: Queue depth rises BEFORE TTFT does, because a request has to wait before it can be slow. This is the leading indicator: sustained depth above ~3 means arrivals exceed service rate and shedding is imminent.

panels.title: Why requests were shed
panels.description: 'We are full' and 'you personally are using too much' are different problems with different fixes, so they are counted separately. per_key_limit rising alone means one tenant is misbehaving while the service is fine.

panels.title: Engine signals that predict capacity loss
Prefix cache hit rate — THE capacity signal
panels.description: The KV cache is one shared pool of ~69,760 tokens, not a per-user allocation. When the working set of active conversations stops fitting, hit rate collapses and every turn re-prefills its whole history at roughly 9x the cost of a hit. This falls BEFORE latency rises, because spare capacity absorbs the extra prefill first — which is what makes it predictive rather than merely descriptive.

panels.title: KV cache usage and preemptions
panels.description: Normal operation for this deployment is 8-17%. Preemption means the engine evicted a running sequence and will recompute it, so throughput is being spent twice on the same tokens. Metric name is kv_cache_usage_perc — gpu_cache_usage_perc was guessed once in this project and produced a panel that silently showed nothing.

panels.title: Engine concurrency and throughput
panels.description: Running should track the gateway's in-flight count closely. If running is persistently lower, something between the gateway and the engine is the constraint; if waiting is non-zero, the engine's own scheduler is queueing behind --max-num-seqs, which for this deployment is set to 32 precisely so it never binds before the gateway does.

panels.title: Context trimming
panels.description: Non-zero means conversations are outgrowing the 32,768-token window and the gateway is dropping their oldest turns to keep them alive. Each trim is also a guaranteed prefix-cache miss, because the hash chain is invalidated from the first changed block onward — so a rise here should be visible as a dip in hit rate above.

panels.title: Errors: upstream failures and billing write failures
panels.description: Billing write failures are critical rather than cosmetic: non-zero means GPU work is being served that cannot be accounted for. The budget CHECK fails closed (refuse new work); the budget WRITE fails soft (never damage a response that already succeeded), and this counter is what makes the soft failure visible instead of silent.
